items.followUp: State the second condition of equilibrium and write its mathematical form.

rubric.why: Identifies the defining balance of forces for an equilibrium body.
rubric.description: Defines equilibrium in terms of balanced forces.
rubric.how: Award 2 marks for stating that the resultant (net) force on a body in equilibrium is zero.

rubric.why: States the first condition and its meaning.
rubric.description: Gives the first condition of equilibrium and explains it.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the condition that the vector sum of forces is zero and 1 mark for identifying this as translational equilibrium (no linear acceleration).

modelAnswer: A body is in equilibrium when the resultant force and resultant torque acting on it are zero.
The first condition of equilibrium is that the vector sum of all forces acting on the body is zero: ΣF = 0.
This condition is called translational equilibrium; the body has no linear acceleration.

items.followUp: Define a prefix and give the meaning and symbol of the prefix milli-.

rubric.why: Captures that a prefix modifies a unit by a specified factor.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining that a prefix is placed before a unit to show a power-of-ten multiple or submultiple.

rubric.why: Provides a valid prefix and its value.
rubric.description: Gives an example of a prefix.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct example, such as kilo = 1000 (10³); accept another correctly stated prefix and value.

modelAnswer: A prefix is a word or symbol placed before a unit to show a multiple or submultiple of that unit by a power of ten.
For example, kilo (k) means 1000, so 1 kilometre = 1000 metres.

items.followUp: Give one example each of a scalar quantity and a vector quantity.

rubric.why: Distinguishes vectors by their direction as well as magnitude.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that a vector quantity has both magnitude and direction.

rubric.why: Identifies a scalar by the absence of direction.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that a scalar quantity has magnitude only.

modelAnswer: A vector is a physical quantity that has both magnitude and direction, for example, displacement.
A scalar is a physical quantity that has magnitude only, for example, distance.

items.followUp: Name the SI units of length, mass and time.

rubric.why: Identifies SI as the internationally agreed system of units.
rubric.description: States what SI stands for or represents.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying SI as the International System of Units.

rubric.why: Explains the purpose of using a common system.
rubric.description: States that SI provides standard units for measurements.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining that it is a standard system used internationally for measurements.

modelAnswer: The International System of Units (SI) is the internationally agreed standard system of units used for measurements.
It provides common units for physical quantities throughout the world.

items.followUp: Define displacement and give an example showing its direction.

rubric.why: Shows that position specifies where an object is relative to a reference.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for defining position as the location of an object with respect to a reference point.

rubric.why: Gives a location using a reference point and a stated direction or distance.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a valid example, such as a book 2 m east of a table or a car 10 m from a reference point.

modelAnswer: Position is the location of an object with respect to a reference point.
For example, a book may be 2 m east of a table taken as the reference point.

items.followUp: Can an object moving in a circle at constant speed be accelerating? Explain briefly.

rubric.why: Gives the correct conclusion that acceleration is possible at constant speed.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that a body moving at constant speed can have acceleration.

rubric.why: Explains that changing direction changes velocity, producing acceleration.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining that acceleration occurs when direction changes, for example during circular motion.

modelAnswer: Yes, a body moving at constant speed can have acceleration.
In circular motion its direction changes continuously, so its velocity changes and it has centripetal acceleration.

items.followUp: A force of 20 N acts perpendicular to an area of 4 m². Calculate the pressure.

rubric.why: Defines pressure as force acting per unit area.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that pressure is force per unit area (perpendicular to the surface).

rubric.why: Gives the correct SI unit of pressure.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for pascal (Pa), equivalent to N/m².

modelAnswer: Pressure is the perpendicular force acting per unit area of a surface.
Its SI unit is the pascal (Pa), where 1 Pa = 1 N/m².

items.followUp: A wire of original length 2 m is stretched by 0.01 m. Calculate its tensile strain.

rubric.why: Gives the definition of tensile strain as extension divided by original length.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating tensile strain = change in length/original length.

rubric.why: Explains that strain is a ratio of lengths and therefore has no unit.
rubric.description: Explains why tensile strain has no unit.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining that the length units in the numerator and denominator cancel, leaving a dimensionless quantity.

modelAnswer: Tensile strain is the change in length of a body divided by its original length: tensile strain = ΔL/L.
It has no unit because both quantities are lengths measured in the same unit, so their units cancel.
